newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Oct 31.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Financial Times - Oct 31.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
-- CLARKE SURPRISES CITY WITH RISE IN BANK BASE RATES

Chancellor Kenneth Clarke has raised UK base rates by a quarter point, to 6 per cent. The surprise move followed concern by the Bank of England after Clarke's last rate cut four months ago. The Bank welcomed news of Wednesday's rise, claiming it has improved the chancellor's chances of hitting his inflation target of 2.5 per cent or less in the medium term.
-- BAA MAY PAY 500M STG IN LABOUR WINDFALL TAX PLAN

A report by the Financial Times claims that airports operator BAA could face a much higher-than-expected windfall tax bill if it is included in the list of companies targeted by Labour's planned utility levy. The paper's calculations suggest that BAA could face a bill of over 500m stg, based on the Labour party's public statements about the windfall tax.
-- KOPPER TO STAND DOWN AS DEUTSCHE BANK CHAIRMAN

Hilmar Kopper, chairman of Germany's biggest bank Deutsche Bank, is to step down from the position next May. The move comes several years before Kopper reaches the bank's normal retirement age of 65, but has been welcomed as a positive step by analysts. Rolf Breuer, currently a director at the Bank, is to succeed him. During Kopper's seven year tenure in the post Deutsche Bank has been linked to several scandal-hit German companies.
-- ITALIAN TELECOMS SELL-OFF SET TO BE POSTPONED

The Italian treasury has admitted that the privatisation of Italy's state-controlled telecoms holding company Stet, which has been subject to political wrangling over how the sale should proceed, is unlikely to take place by the deadline of March 1997. Most of the problems with the sale of Stet centre on Italy's failure to establish a telecoms regulator, and a further delay is likely to disconcert international investors as well as damage Italy's relations with the European Commission.
-- BEEF AID PACKAGE CLEARS WAY FOR WIDER MEASURES

European Union farm ministers have reached agreement on a package of aid for beef farmers, clearing the way for measures to cut surplus stock. The breakthrough came after EU Agriculture Commissioner Franz Fischler agreed to additional aid of Ecu500m (390m stg) to be paid to beef farmers in 1997. The short-term measures are to be supplemented with deeper reforms in the future, and the ministers called on Fischler to submit proposals on further changes within six months.
-- GIORDANO URGES CHANGES IN GAS WATCHDOG REGIME

British Gas chairman Richard Giordano has called for changes in the way monopoly utilities are regulated. Speaking before the Commons select committee on trade and industry, Giordano accused the gas industry watchdog Ofgas of being 'erratic', and claimed that the present regulatory system gives too much power to a single individual.
-- DIXONS IN $1.5M ROW OVER 6 STG SALE

High Street consumer electronics retailer Dixons is involved in a David and Goliath legal wrangle after a London-based computer consultant and commodities dealer sued the company for $1.5m in damages. The claim relates to a 6 stg cable splitter which the plaintiff, Richard Wood, bought from Dixons and which he alleges was faulty and caused his business system to collapse. Dixons has admitted the cable was faulty, but disputes a court's decision to award an interim payment of 22,000 stg.
-- SAINSBURY SPEEDS UP BOARD CHANGES

Supermarket and retail group J. Sainsbury has brought forward a boardroom shake-up by announcing it will appoint Dino Adriano as chief executive of the supermarkets business in March, rather than at the end of 1997. Adriano will replace Tom Vyner in a move to stem criticism of management following the success of rivals Tesco in taking a market lead over the company in the past year.
-- LVMH AGREES TO BUY STAKE IN DUTY FREE CHAIN

French luxury goods group LVMH has announced that it has reached a conditional agreement on a $2.47bn (1.58bn stg) deal to acquire a majority stake in the duty-free shopping chain DFS. LVMH had hoped to buy all of DFS for $4.2bn, but was only able to agree terms with two of the four shareholders in the privately- owned company. The other two shareholders have now filed legal action to block the deal.
-- PROTON TO PAY 51M STG FOR 80 PER CENT OF LOTUS

Malaysian vehicle producer Proton has unveiled details of its plans for British carmaker Lotus, after confirming a 51m stg deal to acquire an 80 per cent stake in the Norfolk-based sports car and engineering group. Proton plans a programme of rapid expansion at Lotus, including the production of Lotus models at Proton plants in Malaysia. The Asian company, which is investing 1bn stg to raise its output to 500,000 units a year by 1999, plans to produce a range of vehicles in niche sectors, including sports cars, 4-wheel drives and MPVs.
